newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Poverty grows in Argentina's largest urban area.
newsitem.headline: Poverty grows in Argentina's largest urban area.

text.p: Argentina has returned to the path of economic growth, but a year-long recession just ended has left the nation with more poverty and hunger, official data shows.

Economy Ministry figures released late Wednesday showed the number of poor on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, the country's largest urban area, grew to 3.7 million in May from 3.1 million a year earlier.
More embarrassing still for a major beef and grain producing country, the number of indigents, or extremely poor, grew to 7.2 percent of the area's population from 5.4 percent.
In its quarterly report on the state of the economy, the ministry said it believed those figures were the result of a rise in staple food prices and to joblessness.
Unemployment currently stands at 17 percent, compared with only seven percent when President Carlos Menem first took office in 1989.
The poverty figures cast a shadow over brighter data in the same report: 2.6 percent economic growth in the second quarter, marking the end of a 12-month-long recession.
After growing at a rate of 7.7 percent over the past few years, the economy shrank 4.6 percent in 1995 after being hit by the "tequila effect" of the Mexican peso devaluation.

So far, government policy both in good times and bad has been more austerity. But both the population at large and unions, the ruling Peronist Party's traditional allies, seem to be growing impatient.
The latest opinion poll conducted in September showed Menem, who in May 1995 won a second term with 50 percent of the vote, had only a 14 percent backing.

And unions, which staged two general strikes in the past two months and are considering new action, Wednesday declined to show up for talks with ruling Peronist legislators after finding out that cabinet ministers would also be attending.

A labor leader told the daily Clarin newspaper that they cancelled the meeting because they considered it a government tactic to show the two sides were discussing official plans to loosen labor legislation, which unions oppose.

The new laws would put an end to forced collecive bargaining, letting firms negotiate directly with workers, and mean smaller severance payments, more flexible working hours and even wages tied to company performance.

"They want to take us back to the turn of the century," Rodolfo Daer, leader of the main CGT union federation, protested last Monday after Menem signed a decree aimed at taking health care control away from unions.
